post.title: A Mac guard for AI coding tools
post.promise: See and control what coding agents can access on a Mac.
post.whatItIs: Plango describes a Mac security product with controls for coding agent access, MCP servers, skills and plugins, plus secret handling and connection monitoring. A beginner could hypothetically prototype a narrow checklist that helps a Mac user review agent permissions; it would not itself secure the computer.
post.whoPays: Plango advertises a subscription. A separate beginner checklist service would need to test whether Mac developers would pay; that demand is only a hypothesis.
loop: User lists the coding agents and folders they use.
A form asks which files or connections they want to restrict.
A simple rules checklist maps answers to review prompts.
The user checks the suggestions against actual Mac settings.
A person approves every access change and tests it manually.
post.evidence: Plango's site describes agent access controls, MCP server visibility, skill and plugin checks, moving plain text keys into Keychain, connection monitoring and Mac requirements. It lists $4.99 per month and a seven day free trial.
post.uncertainty: These are claims on Plango's own site, not independently verified outcomes. The proposed checklist is hypothetical and cannot inspect or protect a Mac automatically; a person must verify settings and avoid exposing secrets.
first24Hours: Read Plango's feature and system requirement pages.
Draft a one page checklist for reviewing one coding agent's file access.
Ask one Mac developer to check whether the prompts are understandable; do not request credentials or sensitive files.

ease.reason: A permission checklist is a small first experiment, though useful Mac security guidance requires careful domain learning.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: Mac developers might pay for clearer agent permission reviews; the source lists Plango pricing but does not validate demand for a checklist.

feasibility.reason: A static checklist can be prototyped in four weeks, but the source's access controls and protection claims are beyond that narrow version.

autonomy.reason: A form can organize answers, while users must verify settings and approve every security change.

evidence.reason: The first party site describes the working product and features, but supplies no independent real use evidence.

post.title: Plango watches AI agents on your Mac
post.promise: Review agent activity, connections and access from one Mac security app.
post.whatItIs: Plango describes a Mac security app for developers using coding agents. Its page says it can watch agent actions, show MCP server connections, scan skills and plugins, and let people set rules for events and requests.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers who want visibility into local AI agent activity might pay for this kind of Mac security tool. The page lists a subscription, but does not establish customer demand.
loop: Install the app on a compatible Apple silicon Mac running macOS 15 or newer.
Connect or use a coding agent supported by the product.
Review the events, requests, decisions and blocks Plango displays.
Set rules for agent access or connections that you want to control.
Check blocked actions and adjust rules yourself when needed.
post.evidence: The attached product page describes agent monitoring, MCP visibility, skill and plugin checks, access controls, and an event view with configurable rules. It lists a seven-day trial and a $4.99 monthly subscription, and specifies compatible Mac requirements.
post.uncertainty: This is the product maker's own description, not independent evidence of security effectiveness or customer use. People still need to judge alerts, set appropriate rules, and decide whether to allow actions; the page does not establish that every risk is detected.
first24Hours: Check whether your Mac meets the stated Apple silicon, macOS and memory requirements.
Read the product's terms and privacy information before creating an account.
If you try it, review the event view and note which decisions still need your judgment.

ease.reason: The page gives a trial and signup path, but the experiment requires a compatible Apple silicon Mac and agent setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: developers concerned about agent access could be buyers; the listed subscription does not show demand or sales.

feasibility.reason: A four-week review of the app's event view is plausible, though compatibility and actual security performance need checking.

autonomy.reason: The page describes ongoing monitoring and rule-based blocks, while people must configure rules and assess alerts.

evidence.reason: The first-party page describes product features and trial access, but supplies no independent working demonstration or real-use evidence.

post.title: Turn project notes into a reviewed brief
post.promise: Try a local assistant workflow that drafts a project brief for you to check.
post.whatItIs: Kucedr presents a desktop assistant for writing, research, coding and media tasks, with local files, configurable model providers and scheduled tasks that require the app to stay open. Its site shows a demo saving an artwork selection, copy, layout and palette as a brief. A student could hypothetically test a similar brief-making workflow with sample notes.
post.whoPays: Kucedr offers downloads and says its cloud service is coming soon. A student version's buyer and willingness to pay are hypothetical and untested.
loop: Choose a fictional project and provide non-sensitive notes.
Ask the assistant to extract the project name, goal and open questions.
Generate a short brief with those fields and source notes.
Compare every field with the original notes.
Edit or discard unsupported details before sharing the brief.
post.evidence: Kucedr's site describes a desktop assistant for macOS, Linux and Windows, configurable providers, local profile and files, and scheduled tasks that run while Kucedr remains open. Its embedded example shows saving artwork, copy, layout and palette into a brief, with date and venue still to add.
post.uncertainty: The product details and example come from Kucedr's own site. The example does not establish accuracy across other projects. The student workflow is hypothetical; a person must check facts, privacy and missing details before sharing or scheduling anything.
first24Hours: Review Kucedr's getting started information and supported desktop platforms.
Use fictional notes to outline a five field project brief.
Manually compare a draft brief with its sample notes and mark any unsupported or missing fields.

ease.reason: The site describes a desktop workflow and a concrete saved brief demo that a beginner can inspect and imitate with sample notes.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: people coordinating small projects might value brief drafting, but the source gives no evidence of paying customers or demand for this adaptation.

feasibility.reason: A draft-and-review brief using sample notes fits a four-week experiment; trustworthy integration across users' tools would be a larger task.

autonomy.reason: Drafting can be repeated from notes, but the source's example leaves date and venue incomplete and a human must check content.

evidence.reason: The first party page describes the product and shows a working brief example, but does not establish outside use or accuracy.

Ask for an initial image or draft, then inspect the result.
Request alternatives and choose a direction yourself.
Ask for supporting copy or layout suggestions.
Save a brief and fill in missing details before handing it to a person.

Download Kucedr for your operating system and connect a provider if you decide to try it.

ease.reason: The page gives a download path and a concrete poster workflow, but use requires a model/provider choice and task setup.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: creators or small teams might pay for drafting help, but the attached page provides no buyer or revenue evidence.

feasibility.reason: A beginner can try the shown poster-to-brief workflow in four weeks using the listed desktop downloads and a bounded creative task.

No API key. Self-hosted. Over MCP. Your agent calls google_search and gets Google's actual results page as typed JSON: every link resolved to its real URL, plus the AI Overview, People also ask and related searches. A real Firefox ( Camoufox ) runs Google's page as it is, on your own IP or through any proxy you already have. Why: plain HTTP gets a JavaScript wall, automated Chrome got a CAPTCHA 2 out of 2 times in our test, and Google's official Custom Search API closes on 1 January 2027. Other search MCP servers either aren't Google's index (Brave, Tavily, Exa, DuckDuckGo) or charge per query (SerpApi, Bright Data). A real, live call on a home IP with a warm session, rendered from the recorded result; the wait shown is the measured time. MP4 🚀 Quick start uv tool install gsearch-agent # or: pipx install gsearch-agent gsearch setup # downloads the browser once (~1 GB), prints your MCP config claude mcp add gsearch --scope user -- gsearch-mcp # or any MCP client, below Then just ask: "Search Google for what asyncio is and give me the top three links" , "What do people also ask about asyncio?" , "Find asyncio pages on python.org from the past year." Without a proxy, gsearch uses your own IP, at most 20 searches an hour. For more, add a proxy in any format: claude mcp add gsearch --scope user -e GSEARCH_PROXY= " gate.example.com:7000:user-sid-{sid}:password " -e GSEARCH_DATA_LIMIT_MB=1000 -- gsearch-mcp Claude Desktop, Cursor and other MCP clients gsearch setup prints this block with the full path of gsearch-mcp filled in. Use the full path if your client doesn't find the command. { "mcpServers" : { "gsearch" : { "command" : " gsearch-mcp " , "env" : { "GSEARCH_PROXY" : " optional, any format " , "GSEARCH_DATA_LIMIT_MB" : " 1000 " } } } } Claude Desktop: claude_desktop_config.json . Cursor: ~/.cursor/mcp.json , or .cursor/mcp.json in a project. No install, with uv: use "command": "uvx", "args": ["gsearch-agent"] , after fetching the browser once with uvx --from gsearch-agent gsearch setup . Settings in a file: put them in a .env (see .env.example ) and set GSEARCH_ENV_FILE to its absolute path instead. Note Automated access to Google Search may breach Google's Terms of Service. Read Legal and responsible use before running live searches. 🆚 How it compares The same comparison as text gsearch SerpApi, Bright Data Brave, Tavily, Exa DuckDuckGo, SearXNG MCPs Playwright + Chromium Google MCPs Google's own results ✅ ✅ ❌ their own index ❌ / depends on the instance ✅ API key or account none required required none none Cost free (+ your proxy, optional) per query usage-based plans free free Runs on your machine ✅ ❌ hosted ❌ hosted ✅ ✅ AI Overview, People also ask ✅ ✅ (SerpApi) ❌ ❌ varies Google's redirect links resolved to real URLs ✅ ✅ n/a n/a varies Blocks reported as errors with a retry time ✅ n/a n/a varies varies Terms-of-Service risk is yours yes ( Legal ) the provider's no low yes "Varies": we did not test those projects. Our only Chromium measurement is F-0001 : Playwright Chrome was sent to a CAPTCHA 2 of 2 times on an IP where gsearch was served. Read Legal before running live searches. Measured in October 2026: F-0014 , F-0006 , F-0011 , F-0012 , F-0001 ; 14 s and 0.6 MB on a clean proxy IP: F-0015 . Flagged proxy pools are slower: see Performance . ✨ Why gsearch Google's official search API is closed to new customers and shuts down on 1 January 2027 ( F-0005 ). gsearch is built for AI agents instead: 🦊 A real browser, not a scraper. Camoufox, a hardened Firefox, runs Google's page as it is, with a real-device fingerprint and a locale that matches its IP. 🔗 Real URLs. Google hides result links behind /goto redirects. gsearch resolves every one to the page it points to, without loading that page. 🤖 Built for agents. One MCP server, two tools, typed JSON. Blocks come back as clear errors with retry_after_s , never as empty results, and every string is flagged as untrusted web content. 🌍 Any proxy, any format. Rotating residential, static VPS or datacenter lists, HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS5, in any common layout. Every byte is counted, with a hard data limit. 🎯 Nothing to tune. Two settings. Everything else is fixed to what worked best in testing. 📊 Honest numbers. post.title: Review search results before an agent uses them
post.promise: Explore a search workflow with a human review step built in.
post.whatItIs: Gsearch's repository describes a self-hosted MCP server that uses Firefox to retrieve Google results for AI agents, including resolved result URLs and typed JSON. A beginner could hypothetically prototype a manual research log that records search questions and lets a person check links before use. The prototype would not automate Google access.
post.whoPays: The repository describes Gsearch as self-hosted and says no API key is required. Whether developers would pay for a separate reviewed research workflow is hypothetical and untested.
loop: Write a research question and record its purpose.
Run a search only after checking applicable service terms and access rules.
Record the returned result titles and destination URLs.
Open each candidate page and check that it supports the intended point.
A person decides which source, if any, an agent may use.
post.evidence: The repository README describes Gsearch as a self-hosted Google search MCP using Firefox and returning results as typed JSON. It documents a live-call demonstration and cautions that automated Google access may breach Google's Terms of Service.
post.uncertainty: These are repository claims and demonstrations, not independent checks of reliability or permission. Google access has an explicit terms risk. The proposed manual log does not automate searches; people must confirm terms, inspect pages and reject unsupported or unsafe material.
first24Hours: Read the repository's legal and responsible use section before considering live use.
Create a manual research log template with question, result URL and support notes.
Populate it using saved or otherwise permitted example material and have a person verify each claim against its page.

ease.reason: A manual research log is approachable, but the documented live workflow requires installing a browser-based server and careful terms review.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: developers might value reviewed research notes, but the repository offers no evidence of paying demand for that service.

feasibility.reason: A manual log and review prototype fits four weeks; automating live Google searches carries a terms risk the README explicitly flags.

autonomy.reason: The safe proposed log is mostly manual, and a person must verify sources and decide what an agent can use.

evidence.reason: The repository gives implementation details and a live-call demonstration, while its claims are first-party and do not establish independent real use.

post.title: Gsearch gives agents Google result data
post.promise: A self-hosted search tool returns result links and related Google page content to an AI agent.
post.whatItIs: Gsearch is a public repository for an MCP server, a way for an AI tool to call another tool. Its README says it uses a Firefox-based browser to retrieve Google results and returns typed JSON, including resolved result URLs and, when present, AI Overview and related questions.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: developers who want Google results in an agent workflow might pay for support or related services, but the repository describes the tool as self-hosted and no API key required; it gives no buyer evidence.
loop: Read the repository's legal and responsible-use guidance before trying live searches.
Install the package using one of the README's listed methods and run its setup.
Connect the MCP server to a compatible agent using the generated configuration.
Ask a bounded search question and inspect the returned links and text.
Check the sources yourself and stop if access is blocked or use is not appropriate.
post.evidence: The attached public repository README describes installation, setup, MCP client configuration and a live search example. It says results include resolved URLs and typed fields, reports a limit of up to 20 searches per hour without a proxy, and warns that automated access may breach Google's terms.
post.uncertainty: These are repository claims and demonstration details, not independent verification of reliability. The README explicitly places terms-of-service risk on the user. A human must review source quality, legal and policy constraints, and any search results before relying on them.
first24Hours: Read the repository's legal and responsible-use guidance and decide whether a test is appropriate.
Review the setup instructions and requirements before installing anything.
If you proceed, try one low-stakes query and manually verify each result from its destination page.

ease.reason: The README provides setup instructions, but installation includes downloading a browser and configuring an MCP client.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: agent developers might value this workflow, but the README describes a self-hosted tool and supplies no buyer evidence.

feasibility.reason: A small four-week test is technically bounded by the documented setup and one search flow, with browser setup and access constraints to resolve.

autonomy.reason: The server automates browser retrieval and structured output, but humans must check results and judge legal and access limits.

evidence.reason: The repository supplies setup instructions and a live-call demonstration, but its performance claims are maker-reported and not independently checked here.
